content: Late congenital syphilis is a specific form of congenital syphilis that manifests in children who are two years of age or older. This condition arises when the infection is transmitted transplacentally from the mother to the fetus during pregnancy. The clinical features of late congenital syphilis include the following: Blunted upper incisor teeth, which are referred to as Hutchinson's teeth. Inflammation of the cornea, a condition known as interstitial keratitis. Hearing loss caused by auditory nerve damage. Frontal bossing, which is the prominence of the brow ridge. Saddle nose, characterized by the collapse of the bony structure of the nose. Defects in the hard palate. Swollen knees. Saber shins, which describe anterior bowing of the tibia. A shortened maxilla (upper jaw). A protruding mandible (lower jaw). A commonly observed combination of symptoms in late congenital syphilis is known as Hutchinson's triad. This triad consists of Hutchinson's teeth (notched incisors), interstitial keratitis, and deafness. Hutchinson's triad is present in approximately 63% of cases. Timely treatment with penicillin, administered before the onset of late-stage symptoms, is critical to prevent the development of these complications.
